title: Not inflamed
hook: not knowing the eye as it is, one is inflamed; knowing it, one is free

segments.voice: Yesterday: anatta, and your line, not self, six times. Did a feeling arrive through one door and leave again? Today, what happens when we don't see those doors clearly. Day five hundred fourteen.

A bakery window at the end of a long day. Glazed pastries under warm light, a cake with a perfect swirl. The glass hasn't changed since morning, and the person walking past hadn't wanted cake a minute ago. Now there's heat, a pull, a little restlessness. The hundred and forty-ninth discourse has a word for that state. The Pali is saratta, usually rendered inflamed, or impassioned. And it says the fire doesn't start in the cake or the window. It starts in how things are seen. Today: not inflamed.
screen: `A BAKERY WINDOW, LATE.` → `A SUDDEN PULL.` → `SARATTA: INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the great six sense bases, and it begins with a contrast. When someone doesn't know and see the eye as it actually is, the Buddha says, and doesn't know forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and the feeling that comes from it as they actually are, they become inflamed by lust for all of it. Inflamed, tied up, infatuated, fixed on the sweetness. And then things build. Craving grows. The heaps of clinging pile up for the future. Troubles of body and mind grow, torments grow, fevers grow. And the person feels it, in the body and in the mind. Now the other side. When someone knows and sees the eye as it actually is, and the forms, and the seeing, they aren't inflamed. Craving fades. The heaps of clinging shrink. The fevers go down. And the text says this person feels ease, in body and in mind. The key phrase is yathabhuta: as it actually is. Not as advertised, not as feared. Just as it is. Notice what's not being blamed. Not the eye. Not the world. The eye is fine. The cake is fine. The problem is the fog between them. And then a surprise. For a person who sees this way, the text says, their view simply is right view, their intention right intention, their effort right effort. The eightfold path, the text says, comes to fulfillment in them. Calm and insight, it says, run together, evenly yoked. Like two oxen under one yoke, pulling one cart.
screen: `NOT SEEING CLEARLY: INFLAMED` · `CRAVING GROWS, FEVERS GROW` · `SEEING AS IT ACTUALLY IS` · `THE PATH FULFILLS ITSELF` · then, large: `NOT INFLAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know one sense clearly. Rest one hand on something near you: a sleeve, a table, your own knee. First just texture and temperature. Then notice whether there's a small liking or disliking, a pull toward it or away. Don't fix it. Just name it: liking, or not liking, or neither. Now let the hand go still and rest with whatever's left of the touch. Notice the temperature of the mind. Is it warm, cool, still? The bell holds the time.
Not inflamed. Seeing the senses as they actually are, yathabhuta, so the pull of what's seen doesn't set the mind on fire. Today's word.
Your line: two oxen under one yoke. Today, when something in a window or on a screen pulls at you, pause and see it as it is: light, color, a little wanting. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Theravada meditators practice sense restraint and bare noticing, seeing what comes through each sense as it actually is; teachers often pair this with calm practice so that, as MN 149 says, calm and insight develop together.

myth: MN 149 says the eye itself is the problem
the eye is fine. the problem is not knowing it, and what it sees, as it actually is.
the text says clear seeing brings ease in body and mind
fevers and torments go down, and the person feels ease.
for someone who sees clearly, the eightfold path is said to come to fulfillment
their view simply is right view, their effort right effort, and so on.

fork.setup: a beautiful thing catches your eye and the old heat starts to rise. what does MN 149 point to?
options: see the eye, the thing and the feeling as they actually are.
never look at anything beautiful again.
get the thing quickly so the heat stops.
fork.reveal: the discourse doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes. it asks them to see clearly, and says the inflaming fades when they do.

original.note: Pali yathabhuta: as it actually is, as it has come to be. the key to not being inflamed.

trapdoor: what you thought: not inflamed means not getting angry.
what it means: not set on fire by craving for what the senses bring.
what a scholar hears: MN 149 links clear seeing of the six bases directly to the eightfold path and to calm and insight 'yoked evenly', a key text for how the two kinds of meditation fit together.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 149, Mahasalayatanika Sutta (the great discourse on the six sense bases)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook rewritten: it told the listener what they feel ('you feel strangely hot') and repeated the screen/tabs image of days 504-505; 'saratta: dyed' etymology cut (now 'usually rendered inflamed'); 'the path comes to fulfillment almost on its own' overstated the text; 'Picture' line changed; practice moved from sight to touch so it doesn't repeat days 512 and 517.
MN 149 paraphrased. Confirm the Pali saratta ('inflamed / dyed with lust') and the sequence: craving grows, the five aggregates of clinging build up, troubles, torments and fevers grow.

Confirm that the text says right action, speech and livelihood were 'already purified' and that calm and insight are described as yoked evenly (yuganaddha); the oxen image is an explanatory gloss, not the text's own simile.
The scrolling scene in the hook is a modern illustration, not from the text.
